11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A schema property** — when the lesson is about a document's *shape*: a field that must be present, a
59	   value from a closed set, a type, a key set nothing may extend. It belongs in the JSON Schema the document
60	   points at with `$schema` (created from the first such rule where the document has none), which an editor
61	   shows while the document is written and the engine's `schema-conformance` check enforces for every such
62	   document at once. Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there: a declared `checkParsedFiles`
63	   assertion over a field, or a coded rule re-reading a document's shape by hand, is a schema check in
64	   disguise. Only what a schema cannot say — a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the
65	   tree — goes on to the rungs below.
66	2. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
67	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. Declare it at the moment its signature
68	   lives: a **world** check over the tree — one pass ("these patterns over these files"), or two when a value
69	   read in one place must agree with, exist in or be absent from another (`extractValueSets` derives the set,
70	   `checkSetValues`/`checkSetPairs`/`requireIdenticalFiles` quantify over it); a **work** check over the
71	   change (`scope: "work"` — the lines it adds or removes, a co-change, an untracked file, the session's
72	   declared comment classes); or an **action** guard on a tool call (`scope: "action"`, `guardToolCalls` —
73	   denied or nudged at PreToolUse, backstopped over the transcript at Stop). Most captured conditions are
74	   one of these, and a lesson about *how an operation is performed* is usually the third. Give it
75	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
76	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
77	   else's next change, not this run's.
78	3. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
79	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
80	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
81	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
82	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
83	4. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure or a bias rather than a condition —
84	   and name the moment it must load under its `metadata`: `force-load-on-file-edits-paths`,
85	   `force-load-on-tool-calls` (opening a PR, committing, merging, fetching), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`
86	   (an owner's command phrase) or `force-load-on-tool-results-matching` (a symptom in a result). A skill
87	   with no trigger loads on description alone, which is model discretion; a procedure keyed to an act has a
88	   call to name, and rules sharing a trigger belong in one skill so one load carries the whole procedure.
89	5. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
90	
91	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
92	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
93	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
94	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
95	
96	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
97	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
98	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
99	
100	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
101	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small** — a pass adds at most two rules, each one
102	sentence. How a rule is phrased and sized, and where its rationale goes — the brief rule in `RULES.md`, the
103	reaffirmable reason in the pack's `references.md` — is the
104	[writing-pack-prose](skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) skill's; load it before writing any. The full
105	evidence trail stays in the PR body and the issue.
106	
107	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
108	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
109	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
110	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
111	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
112	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
113	
114	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
115	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
116	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
117	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
118	basics pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
119	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
120	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
121	
122	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
123	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
124	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
125	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
126	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
127	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
128	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
129	
130	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
131	
132	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
133	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
134	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
135	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.

1. **A schema property** — when the lesson is about a document's *shape*: a field that must be present, a
   value from a closed set, a type, a key set nothing may extend. It belongs in the JSON Schema the document
   points at with `$schema` (created from the first such rule where the document has none), which an editor
   shows while the document is written and the engine's `schema-conformance` check enforces for every such
   document at once. Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there: a declared `checkParsedFiles`
   assertion over a field, or a coded rule re-reading a document's shape by hand, is a schema check in
   disguise. Only what a schema cannot say — a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the
   tree — goes on to the rungs below.
2. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. Declare it at the moment its signature
   lives: a **world** check over the tree — one pass ("these patterns over these files"), or two when a value
   read in one place must agree with, exist in or be absent from another (`extractValueSets` derives the set,
   `checkSetValues`/`checkSetPairs`/`requireIdenticalFiles` quantify over it); a **work** check over the
   change (`scope: "work"` — the lines it adds or removes, a co-change, an untracked file, the session's
   declared comment classes); or an **action** guard on a tool call (`scope: "action"`, `guardToolCalls` —
   denied or nudged at PreToolUse, backstopped over the transcript at Stop). Most captured conditions are
   one of these, and a lesson about *how an operation is performed* is usually the third. Give it
   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
   else's next change, not this run's.
3. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
4. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure or a bias rather than a condition —
   and name the moment it must load under its `metadata`: `force-load-on-file-edits-paths`,
   `force-load-on-tool-calls` (opening a PR, committing, merging, fetching), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`
   (an owner's command phrase) or `force-load-on-tool-results-matching` (a symptom in a result). A skill
   with no trigger loads on description alone, which is model discretion; a procedure keyed to an act has a
   call to name, and rules sharing a trigger belong in one skill so one load carries the whole procedure.
5. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.

Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).

**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).

Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small** — a pass adds at most two rules, each one
sentence. How a rule is phrased and sized, and where its rationale goes — the brief rule in `RULES.md`, the
reaffirmable reason in the pack's `references.md` — is the
[writing-pack-prose](skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) skill's; load it before writing any. The full
evidence trail stays in the PR body and the issue.

When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.

**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
basics pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.

**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.

## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result

Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

    A prune that re-wraps a paragraph, or that deletes a duplicated local check,
    fell outside `under:.claudinite/local/packs && markdown-trims` and parked for a

    the self-widening guard still parks a `task.json` or `merge-rules.json`.
    
    Shrink-only is now `dedup-prune-integrity`'s alone to measure, so its invariant
    gains a character-length arm beside the line count a re-wrap can hide behind.

Author: missingbulb <73882448+missingbulb@users.noreply.github.com>

    product-wiki: qualitative-evidence methodology in writing-wiki-pages (#1947)
    
    * product-wiki: qualitative-evidence methodology in writing-wiki-pages
    
    The pack claims user research as its territory, but only its market and
    competitor halves have a natural public source. Three rules for reading
    qualitative evidence, in the skill both sourcing lanes load and the guard
    forces for every product-wiki/** edit: a quote is attributed to its
    speaker and an asker's or vendor's framing is theirs alone; independent
    voices are counted, not mentions; and a page grounded only in public
    proxies names the proxy and leaves the question it cannot answer
    standing, rather than reading as a finding about this product's users.
    
    That last is the pack's only failure mode that looks healthy to every
    check it has: a user-research page sourced from review sites and
    competitors' testimonials satisfies product-wiki-sources, -page-sections
    and -key-insights while describing other people's customers.
    
    Prompted by a write-up of repurposing Karpathy's LLM-wiki for product
    discovery, whose raw immutable evidence layer was considered and declined
    (no first caller; committed transcripts put customer PII in git history
    permanently; the layer's immutability is unenforceable by checks that
    read the tracked tree). That decision and each rule's reaffirmable reason
    are recorded in the pack's first references.md, and the README names the
    sourcing gap.
    
    No version bump or VERSIONS.md row — the canon's own tasks write those
    after the change lands.
    
    Closes #1946

entries.name: mcp__github__list_pull_requests
entries.description: List pull requests in a GitHub repository. If the user specifies an author, then DO NOT use this tool and use the search_pull_requests tool instead.

fields.description: Subset of fields to return for each pull request. If omitted, all fields are returned. Use this to reduce response size when you only need specific fields; omitting 'body' in particular drops the largest per-result data.

head.description: Filter by head user/org and branch

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)

entries.name: mcp__github__pull_request_read
entries.description: Get information on a specific pull request in GitHub repository.

after.description: Cursor for pagination, used only by the get_review_comments method. Pass the endCursor from the previous page's PageInfo to fetch the next page.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.

{"number":1718,"title":"Retrospective: the executor resolves which pull request a run works on","body":"Not-before: 2026-09-12T11:00:00Z
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: opus

## Subject

#1707, merged 2026-09-05 as `bf06abb`, tracked by #1695; the design is tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6 step 4b and decision §15.32 (`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md`). A task's `expected_outcome` now says what its run does to pull requests — `no_code_changes`, `fresh_pr`, `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr`, `supersede_existing_pr` — and the executor resolves a branch and pull request once, between the precondition's go and code-work, handing it to code-work as `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_*` and to the agent as `Target-branch:` / `Target-pr:` / `Supersedes:` item fields. Eleven canon tasks declare amend or supersede (usage-fold, update, prose-to-checks-sweep, growth-extract, wiki-growth, improve-comments, ci-performance, growth-discover-packs, growth-promote amend; rule-revalidation, growth-dedup supersede).

## The record to read, and each expectation against it

All reads are on this repository through your own GitHub tools; nothing here needs another repository.

- **Executor runs**: `actions_list` on `claudinite-executor.yml`, then `get_job_logs` per run. Each item's resolution prints one line `target — <reason>`; an amend prints `amending #n`, a fallback `has conflicts` or `could not be read`, a supersede `close as superseded once`, a landing `landed #n`.
- **Work items**: closed and open `[claudinite-work]` issues (`task:origin:planned`), their bodies (`Target-branch:`, `Target-pr:`, `Supersedes:`) and converge comments.
- **Pull requests**: the open list and the closed list since the merge; a superseded one carries a comment beginning "Superseded by #"; an amended one has commits after its item's `created_at`.
- **Parks**: open items in `task:status:needs-human-approval` per task, before and after.

Expected amounts over the week:
- `usage-fold` on the canon: one run a day, each `fresh` (its previous fold lands the same run); zero open usage-fold pull requests at any read. An amend here would mean a fold stopped landing.
- `update` on members is outside this read; on the canon `update` runs daily and should never supersede (nothing to supersede on the canon home). Zero `landed #` lines expected here.
- `growth-extract` (daily, amend): on days its previous pull request is still open, the log says `amending #n` and that pull request gains a commit; expect between zero and five amends in the week, and at most one open growth-extract pull request at any read.
- `growth-promote` (daily, amend): same shape; note that pull requests opened before 2026-09-02 lack the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer and are invisible to the resolver, so a promote run may open a fresh pull request beside an old one — that is expected once, not a fault.
- `rule-revalidation` and `growth-dedup` (weekly, supersede): at most one run each; if the previous round's pull request was open and trailered, it closes with the superseding comment once the new one exists.
- Fresh-branch fallbacks (`has conflicts`, `could not be read`): expect zero to two; more than two says amend rarely applies and the reason should be read.
- Failures: zero items parked `needs-human-failure` with `could not be given a target`.

Behaviours expected: no session opens a second pull request beside the one its item names, and no session searches for an open pull request itself (a converge comment or pull request body saying it did is misuse). No worker closes an earlier pull request on its own.

Signals of misuse: an agent session that opened a pull request on a branch other than its `Target-branch:`; a worker reading pull requests to pick a branch; a `Supersedes:` item whose named pull requests are still open after its own delivered.

Signals of overuse: amend applied to a task whose pull request accumulates rounds nobody reviews — the approval-park count for that task rises while no pull request of it merges; the design's answer would be supersede for that task, or a narrower automerge policy.

Signals of a wrong design decision (design alternatives in §15.32): if the fleet's update pull requests pile up unlanded because the green-incumbent landing never fires, the decision to keep landing inside supersede was insufficient; if amends regularly hit "could not be read" mergeability, the three-read poll is too short and the alternative (amend anyway) should be reconsidered; if runs on trailer-less old pull requests keep opening duplicates past the first week, the recognition-by-trailer decision needs a bootstrap sweep.

Cheap to re-examine: the three-read mergeability poll and its two-second wait; which tasks declare amend versus supersede versus fresh (a one-word edit each); the `Retry-every` of this and the verification. Expensive: the four-word vocabulary itself (member declarations carry it), the field names on the item body (stored data), the branch prefix (recognition depends on it).

## Playbook

1. Read when the subject completed from the artifact: #1707's merge commit `bf06abb` on `main` (list_commits or pull_request_read). If less than seven days ago, set `Not-before:` to completion + 7 days, clear the `task:status:*` label, no comment, leave the issue open.
2. Ripe: re-read §15.32 and the expectations above before reading the record, then read the record and answer the four questions — is it working, misused, overused, underused — with counts and links.
3. Findings become issues, one per systemic fault, and this run fixes nothing: an implementation fault is an actionable task issue; a design fault is a discussion issue carrying the evidence and §15.32's alternatives, parked for the owner's decision. Comment the summary here linking each finding, then converge `--outcome done` through `converge-item.mjs`. Four clean answers close the same way, with the summary saying so.
4. A read you cannot make parks `--outcome action` naming exactly which read failed; never convert a blocked read into a verdict.

{"number":1950,"title":"A task declares the pull request it works on, by name — so several tasks can share one","body":"## The problem

The executor's target seam (`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/target.mjs`) keys a task's pull requests on the task's own identity — the branch family `claudinite/<pack>/<task>/`, plus the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer on the head commit as the second recogniser. One task, one family, one standing pull request, by construction. There is no way for a task to say "append to the pull request that already exists", and no way for one task to hand work to another through a pull request.

## The requirement

A task declares **the name of the pull request it works on**. The name is the identity the target seam resolves against, in place of the task id. Tasks declaring the same name share one branch family and therefore one standing pull request; a run appends its commit to whatever is open under that name.

- `pr_name` is optional. **Absent, nothing changes**: the family is `<pack>/<task>` exactly as today, and every existing declaration behaves identically.
- **A literal name, never a pattern.** Nothing expands it and nothing matches it against an existing pull request's text. Two declarations share a pull request when they carry the same string.
- An ad-hoc / `request` task can therefore state the pull request it will land on *before* it runs, and a second task can declare the same name to review or follow up on what the first delivered.

## What it does NOT change

- **A task's properties stay orthogonal.** A declared name does not constrain, and is not constrained by, `automerge`, `expected_outcome`, or anything else. A run tries to auto-merge exactly as it would without a name; a policy that does not cover the accumulated diff does not land it, and the pull request stays open. That is the existing policy engine, not a new rule.
- **Convergence stays per item.** A queue item's own issue is never closed by its pull request merging — `converge-item.mjs` closes or parks it, and an `approval` park stamps `Ends-when: #<pr> closed`, which the janitor's rule G resolves per item. Several items parked on one shared pull request each carry their own `Ends-when:` pointing at it and each close independently.
- **`Claudinite-Task:` stays per commit.** Each run stamps its own, so the movement signals keep telling the project moving from the machinery running. Only the *pull request's* identity becomes shared.

## Scope of this change

- `pr_name` in `task.schema.json` and `task-contract.mjs` (shape validation and the name resolution, nothing cross-field).
- `target.mjs` keyed on the resolved family, with the trailer recogniser kept for the default family only.
- `executor.mjs` passing the family through.
- Tests first, then the docs the two delivery lanes share.

Serialising two runs that resolve one name is #1952, deliberately out of scope here.

Which tasks actually share a name is a follow-up decision, taken once the mechanism exists. The four `claudinite-growth` tasks are **not** candidates — each keeps its own name.

With a family per task, two runs could never resolve the same target: the family *was* the task, and one live item per task is the engine's own invariant. `pr_name` removes that guarantee. Two tasks sharing a name can be picked in the same drain, or by two executor runs at once, and both resolve the same family — each reading the incumbent, each planning an amend or, worse, each planning `fresh` against an empty list and opening a second pull request under one name.

The repo's own rule says where the guard goes: key it on **the target the write lands on**, never the requester's phrasing — so the resolved name, not the item title. The `Blocked-by:` lane is what already serialises work items, and readiness is re-derived by the scheduler's hourly pass, so the shape is likely: at pick, an item whose name is already held by a live item blocks behind it rather than racing it.

The name is a literal string, so there is no clock in it and no boundary case where two runs resolve different names for the same declaration — the comparison is a string equality on the declared value.

Open questions for whoever takes it:

- Is the name available early enough to block on at pick time? The family is resolved by the executor *after* the precondition's go, which may be too late to turn the item around cleanly.
- What a blocked-on-name item does when its blocker parks rather than closes.
- Whether this wants a declarable precondition of its own — "a pull request under my name is already open" — which is a different key from the task-name-based mechanisms that already exist (one live item per task; `last-run-not-failed`). Raised by the owner on #1951.

Until this lands, sharing a name is safe only where the sharing tasks cannot be picked concurrently — a property nothing enforces.

7

9	changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer and less dependent on human steering. Read how the

16	## The goal
17	
18	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
19	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
20	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
21	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
22	
23	## Where the conversation comes from
24	
25	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
26	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
27	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
28	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
29	  A small line-count `offset`/`limit` is not a safe way to `Read` the checked-out file: one JSONL line
30	  can be a single `tool_use`/`tool_result` running tens of thousands of characters, so even a short
31	  window can overflow the read cap. Check line lengths first (e.g. `awk '{print length}' <file> |
32	  sort -n | tail`) or condense the file with a script before attempting a raw read.
33	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
34	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
35	
36	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
37	when a session is done enough to mine.
38	
39	## What to look for — the friction signals
40	
41	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
42	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
43	
44	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
45	
46	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
47	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
48	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
49	
50	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
51	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
52	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
53	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
54	correctly **without the round-trip**.
55	
56	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
57	
58	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
59	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
60	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
61	convention and had it corrected in review.
62	
63	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
64	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
65	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
66	first, not after a detour.
67	
68	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
69	
70	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
71	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
72	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
73	
74	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
75	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
76	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
77	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
78	was already optimal.
79	
80	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
81	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
82	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
83	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
84	loss of quality.
85	
86	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
87	
88	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
89	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
90	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
91	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
92	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
93	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
94	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
95	
96	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
97	
98	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
99	
100	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
101	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
102	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
103	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
104	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
105	
106	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
107	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
108	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
109	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
110	
111	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

113	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
114	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
115	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
116	
117	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
118	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
119	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
120

122	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets

124	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
125	silence it replaced.

---
name: extract-from-conversations
description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
---

# Extract lessons from a conversation

Read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions taken in it — and convert its friction into
changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer and less dependent on human steering. Read how the
work went; what the work committed is [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md)'s.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
  A small line-count `offset`/`limit` is not a safe way to `Read` the checked-out file: one JSONL line
  can be a single `tool_use`/`tool_result` running tens of thousands of characters, so even a short
  window can overflow the read cap. Check line lengths first (e.g. `awk '{print length}' <file> |
  sort -n | tail`) or condense the file with a script before attempting a raw read.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

---
name: running-the-suite
description: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'Bash.command /\bnode\s+--test\b/'
---

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — it reached 37 of 65 files and reported nothing wrong — while `node --test <dir>`
  fails outright, so only the glob leaves you believing a green run. (4)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

input.body:
Refs #1961 — the window's substantive commits were 2ad269d (growth-dedup auto-merges the whole local-pack tree, #1949) and 5fc2e4e (product-wiki qualitative-evidence methodology, #1947). One lesson landed, as a check. No prose rule: the ration went unspent. ## `mount-path-in-the-canon-home` — the vendored path a session here cannot run **The signal.** Both conversations captured in the fresh window ran ``` node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs ``` and got `Cannot find module`, then retried from the repo root. It is not a two-session coincidence: replaying every Bash call on `conversation-logs` through the compiled guard, **14 commands across the corpus** are this mistake — mostly the two sweeps, but also `converge-item.mjs` (2026-08-30) and `session-end-command.mjs` (three times). The canon home carries no `.claudinite/shared/` at all, so each one is a sweep or a convergence the session believed it ran and did not, until it read the error. The path is *correct* prose — it is what `claudinite-lifecycle`'s rules and the queue's instructions spell for a member, and this repo is the one place it never resolves. The local pack already carries the fact in `RULES.md` (26), filed under *writing* a path against the mount; nothing fired when a session went to *run* one. So: an action guard, which is the moment the knowledge is needed. **Why it is confident.** Replayed over all **558 captured sessions rooted in this repo**, it fires on those 14 and on nothing else. The silence is the interesting half, and each arm has a real counter-example behind it: | stays silent | seen in | |---|---| | `cd /home/user/Shepherd && node .claudinite/shared/…` | a cloned member's checkout, which does carry the mount | | `(cd "$T" && … node .claudinite/shared/…)` | the fake-consumer tree a session builds in its scratchpad | | `node .claudinite/shared/… \|\| node engine/…` | the two-root form rule (26) prescribes | | the path inside a heredoc or a `grep` argument | five sessions rewriting member-facing docs | **Evidence trail.** The check's `references.md` entry carries the counts and the retirement condition; the test's negative arms carry the four shapes above, and were proven by weakening `unlessMatches` and watching them bite. ## What did not land - **`pr_name` breaking `pushGenerated`'s force-push premise** (#1953, found reviewing #1951 in the window) — real, but `writing-tasks` already tells an author declaring the field, and this run does not write the canon. - **"an unexercised path is not a clean one"** from the #1718 retrospective — the corpus already says it twice (*a code-search miss is not evidence*; *name an absent field rather than guess it*). - **The hindsight window** (2026-07-19/20, the six oldest captures still on the branch): the friction there — the missing `Comment class:` line in nearly every session, purging a reversed owner decision everywhere, pack independence — is landed and holding; today's captures carry the class line without prompting. ## Folders touched 
.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/  the new action guard's declaration, its rationale
                                    entry, and its fixtures in the action-guards test
The upgrade pass had nothing to convert — this run wrote no prose. Suite: 3435/3436, the one failure the pre-existing shallow-clone guard in `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs`. Work and world sweeps clean. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01DssrwxKBn8KTB5tMxLEGu3

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it
   again. (1)
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
